lead: A closed system can follow many paths between two states. One family obeys pV<sup>n</sup> = C, where p is the pressure, V the volume, n the polytropic index and C a constant. The value of n fixes the process and gives ready formulas for work and heat. Engine cylinders, reciprocating compressors and gas springs follow these paths. This chapter integrates p dV once and then reads the isothermal, adiabatic, isobaric and isochoric processes as special cases.
prereq: You need: the first law and moving boundary work, W = ∫p dV, and the specific heats cv, cp and γ.

blocks.text: A polytropic process follows pV<sup>n</sup> = C, with n a constant pure number. For an ideal gas pV = mRT, so the path also fixes T at every point. The index picks out the familiar processes: n = 0 gives constant pressure (isobaric); n = 1 gives pV constant, which for an ideal gas is constant temperature (isothermal); n = γ = c<sub>p</sub>/c<sub>v</sub> gives the reversible adiabatic; n → ∞ gives constant volume (isochoric). W is work done by the gas and Q heat added to it, so compression has V₂ < V₁ and W < 0.
Put p = C/V<sup>n</sup> into W = ∫p dV from V₁ to V₂ and integrate:

blocks.where: valid for n ≠ 1; p in kPa, V in m³, T in K, m in kg, R in kJ/kg·K, W in kJ, positive when the gas does work.

blocks.text: For n = 1 the denominator is zero, so integrate p = C/V directly:

blocks.where: ln is the natural logarithm. For an ideal gas at constant T, ΔU = 0, so Q = W: in isothermal compression, work goes in and the same amount of heat comes out.

blocks.text: The end states of any polytropic path are linked by p₁V₁<sup>n</sup> = p₂V₂<sup>n</sup> and, for an ideal gas,
put n = γ for the reversible adiabatic. In compression V₁/V₂ > 1, so T₂ > T₁ whenever n > 1.

Adiabatic means Q = 0. For a reversible adiabatic of an ideal gas with constant specific heats the path is pV<sup>γ</sup> = C, and the first law gives W = −ΔU = mc<sub>v</sub>(T₁ − T₂). In compression W < 0 and T rises; in expansion the work comes out of the internal energy and T falls.
For a general polytropic path, find Q from the first law, Q = ΔU + W, or in one line with the polytropic specific heat:
Q = m cn(T₂ − T₁), cn = cv(n − γ)/(n − 1)
c<sub>n</sub> (kJ/kg·K) belongs to the path, not the gas; use it for n ≠ 1. Checks: n = γ gives c<sub>n</sub> = 0 (adiabatic), n = 0 gives c<sub>p</sub>, n → ∞ gives c<sub>v</sub>.

When 1 < n < γ, cn is negative: a compression that heats the gas still rejects heat, and an expansion that cools the gas still takes heat in. On a p-V diagram the adiabatic p = C/Vγ is steeper than the isothermal p = C/V because γ > 1, and a polytropic path with 1 < n < γ lies between them (Figure 2.4.1). The same paths in flow machines are handled with the steady flow energy equation.

figure.caption: The worked examples’ three compressions of 1 kg of air from 0.861 m³ and 100 kPa to one-eighth of the volume, plotted from pVⁿ = C. The adiabatic (n = 1.4) climbs steepest, to 1838 kPa; the polytropic n = 1.3 ends at 1493 kPa and the isothermal at 800 kPa. The area under each curve is the work put in: 279.5, 248.6 and 179.0 kJ.

spec.aria: Pressure against volume for three compression curves from V = 0.861 cubic metres at 100 kPa to V = 0.108 cubic metres: isothermal ending at 800 kPa, polytropic with n = 1.3 ending at 1493 kPa, and adiabatic ending at 1838 kPa, the steepest.

examples.question: 1 kg of air at 300 K and 100 kPa is compressed to one-eighth of its volume. Find the final pressure, final temperature, work and heat if the process is (a) isothermal and (b) reversible adiabatic. Take R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K, c<sub>v</sub> = 0.718 kJ/kg·K, γ = 1.4.
steps: Data: m = 1 kg, T₁ = 300 K, p₁ = 100 kPa, V₁/V₂ = 8. V₁ = mRT₁/p₁ = 0.287 × 300/100 = 0.861 m³, so V₂ = 0.1076 m³.
(a) Isothermal: T₂ = 300 K and p₂ = p₁ × 8 = 800 kPa.
ΔU = 0 for an ideal gas at constant T, so Q = W = −179.0 kJ: 179.0 kJ of heat leaves.
examples.answer: Isothermal: p₂ = 800 kPa, T₂ = 300 K, W = Q = −179.0 kJ. Adiabatic: p₂ = 1838 kPa, T₂ = 689.2 K, W = −279.5 kJ, Q = 0. To the same final volume the adiabatic needs more work because the gas heats up and its pressure climbs faster.

examples.question: The same air (1 kg, 300 K, 100 kPa) is compressed to one-eighth of its volume along pV<sup>1.3</sup> = C. Find p₂, T₂, W, ΔU and Q.
steps: Check with c<sub>n</sub> = 0.718 × (1.3 − 1.4)/0.3 = −0.2393 kJ/kg·K: Q = −0.2393 × 259.8 = −62.2 kJ, the same within rounding (the data 0.718 and 1.4 are each rounded).
examples.answer: p₂ = 1493 kPa, T₂ = 559.8 K, W = −248.6 kJ, ΔU = +186.6 kJ, Q = −62.0 kJ: the gas gets hotter and still rejects heat.

traps: Putting n = 1 into (p₁V₁ − p₂V₂)/(n − 1): it divides by zero. Use the ln formula.
Using γ when the question gives n. A path with n = 1.3 is not adiabatic even though air has γ = 1.4.
Thinking a gas that gets hotter must be receiving heat. With 1 < n < γ the gas heats up and rejects heat, as the second example shows.
For an ideal gas, isothermal means ΔU = 0, not Q = 0; adiabatic means Q = 0, not ΔT = 0.

Comparing paths without saying what is fixed. To the same final volume adiabatic compression needs more work than isothermal (279.5 against 179.0 kJ above); to the same final pressure a closed-system adiabatic needs less, because the volume falls less.

quiz.q: For pV<sup>n</sup> = C, name the process for n = 0, 1, γ and ∞.
quiz.a: Isobaric, isothermal, reversible adiabatic and isochoric.
A process that follows pV<sup>n</sup> = C with n constant along the path.

quiz.q: Why is Q = W in an isothermal process of an ideal gas?
quiz.a: u of an ideal gas depends only on T, so ΔU = 0 when T is constant; Q − W = ΔU then gives Q = W.

quiz.q: 0.5 kg of air at 400 K is compressed isothermally from 100 kPa to 400 kPa (R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K). Find W and Q.
2 kg of air (c<sub>v</sub> = 0.718 kJ/kg·K) is heated at constant volume from 300 K to 400 K. Find W and Q.
quiz.a: V is constant, so W = 0 and Q = ΔU = 2 × 0.718 × 100 = 143.6 kJ.

quiz.q: Why does an adiabatic curve on a p-V diagram fall more steeply than an isothermal one through the same point?
quiz.a: The curves are p = C/V<sup>γ</sup> and p = C/V, with slopes −γp/V and −p/V. Since γ > 1 the adiabatic is steeper: in expansion the gas also cools, so its pressure falls faster.

quiz.q: A compression follows pV<sup>1.2</sup> = C with γ = 1.4. Is heat added or rejected? Use c<sub>n</sub>.
quiz.a: c<sub>n</sub> = c<sub>v</sub>(1.2 − 1.4)/(1.2 − 1) = −c<sub>v</sub>. Compression raises T, so T₂ − T₁ > 0 and Q = m c<sub>n</sub>(T₂ − T₁) < 0: heat is rejected.

beyond: Real reciprocating compressors and engine strokes lie between isothermal and adiabatic because some heat leaks through the cylinder walls, so a measured indicator diagram is fitted with an n between 1 and γ. In turbomachines designers use the polytropic efficiency, the efficiency of an infinitely small stage, which does not change with pressure ratio. Search next for “indicator diagram polytropic index” and “polytropic efficiency compressor”.
